ABSTRACT
This paper presents the design of edge-­triggered PFSCL registers for high-­performance computing systems employed in 
mixed-­signal applications. Two different approaches named as static and dynamic for register design are presented. The static 
approach maintains a constant current flow in the register design throughout the operation. Two static register designs em­
ploying either PFSCL fundamental cells (FC) (SR1) or PFSCL tristate buffers (SR2) are proposed. The proposed static registers 
have high power consumption and gate count. Alternatively, a dynamic register design approach that restricts the current flow 
and facilitates the temporary storage of charge is proposed. Three designs for dynamic PFSCL registers (DR-­1, DR-­2, and DR-­3) 
are proposed. All the proposed PFSCL and existing CMOS registers are implemented and simulated in LTspice with layouts 
drawn in the Microwind tool. The performance comparison indicates that the PFSCL registers show improved performance 
over existing CMOS counterparts at high operating frequency. Further, it is found that the proposed PFSCL DR-­2 register 
achieves the best performance by attaining the maximum improvements of 52.7%, 93.8%, and 97% in propagation delay, power, 
and PDP values at 1 GHz, respectively, as compared to the existing CMOS registers with 59% area overhead. The Monte Carlo 
and corner analysis confirm the stability of the proposed PFSCL registers against process variations and identify the proposed 
DR-­2 register as the least prone design to variations. This paper also addresses the clock overlap issue in the proposed register 
and presents different methods to achieve clock skew insensitivity. Lastly, a 3-­bit shift register implementation is included as 
a design example.
1   |   Introduction
The advancements in integrated circuit technologies have made 
possible the integration of multiple digital and analog functions 
on a single chip for high-­performance computing. It has enabled 
the development of high-­performance computing systems-­on-­a-­
chip (SoC) that are well suited for advanced electronic systems. 
The performance of the SoC has been enhanced in terms of 
speed and density, which are intrinsic in nanometer-­scale inte­
grated circuit processes. However, the integration of analog and 
digital operations on a single chip poses significant difficulties 
in circuit design. The functionality of the analog subsystem is 
severely limited by the large switching noise generated in the 
complementary MOS (CMOS) logic digital subsystem [1–7]. Also, 
CMOS circuits have frequency-­dependent power consumption, 
which increases linearly with the operating frequency. Thus, to 
tackle these difficulties, researchers have investigated alterna­
tive logic styles. One of the promising alternative logic styles is 
the positive feedback source coupled logic (PFSCL) style, which 
operates on the principle of current steering with reduced volt­
age swing. A PFSCL gate has a constant bias current source that 
draws a constant current and hence reduces switching noise and 
accounts for static power consumption independent of operating 
frequency [8–11]. PFSCL circuits are therefore employed in the 
design of digital circuits employed in communication as well as 
arithmetic and logical applications. In literature, various PFSCL

digital circuits such as multiplexers, serializers, D-­latches, razor 
flip-­flops, adders, LFSRs, and tristate buffers are suggested 
[1, 12–20]. However, very little effort has been made toward 
PFSCL register design.
A register plays a key role in digital circuits by performing 
various functions such as data storage, data manipulation, 
and temporary data storage in key applications such as high-­
performance computing used in SoC architectures, digital 
signal processing for filtering, encoding, and decoding, and 
arithmetic unit design [21]. The existing CMOS registers suf­
fer from high switching noise and fail to provide an analog-­
friendly environment in mixed-­signal applications. Also, the 
significant power consumption at high operating frequency 
needs attention. Thus, PFSCL registers are beneficial for such 
applications. However, the study in PFSCL circuit design is 
limited to the design of D-­latch, and no effort has been made 
toward PFSCL register design. Thus, the objective of this paper 
is to implement PFSCL registers. Following are the highlights 
of the work:
1.	 A static PFSCL register design approach that maintains 
constant current flow in the circuit is presented.
2.	 Two static register designs employing either PFSCL funda­
mental cell (FC) [11, 22] or PFSCL tristate buffers [19] are 
proposed.
3.	 The dynamic PFSCL register design approach that restricts 
the flow of current and further lower the power consump­
tion is presented.
4.	 Three different low power dynamic registers with modi­
fied current source section are proposed.
5.	 Different methods to design PFSCL clock skew insensitive 
registers are put forward for completeness.
This paper is organized in five sections, including the 
Introduction section. An overview of the existing PFSCL ­D-­latch 
is presented in Section  2. Different positive edge-­triggered 
PFSCL registers are proposed in Section 3. The Simulation sec­
tion covers the functional verification and performance com­
parison of the proposed and existing positive edge-­triggered 
registers, and the clock overlap issue is analyzed in Section 4. A 
3-­bit shift register is also presented as a design case. In Section 5, 
conclusions are drawn.
2   |   Preliminaries
A D-­latch is extensively used in the design of edge-­triggered 
registers. The available PFSCL D-­latch is implemented by using 
either a PFSCL fundamental cell (FC) [11, 22] or PFSCL tristate 
buffers [19].
2.1   |   PFSCL FC D-­Latch
A PFSCL FC is a circuit element primarily used to implement 
sum-­of-­minterms in a logic function. An FC consists of two 
triple-­tail cells (TTCs) biased by two current sources as shown 
in Figure 1a. The two TTCs, namely, TTC1 (M1, M2, and MF1) 
and TTC2 (M3, M4, and MF2), are driven by inputs X1, X2, and 
X3. The output is obtained by performing wired-­OR among 
any one of the outputs of the two TTCs [(Q1/Q2) and (Q3/Q4)]

through it and the TTC does not influence the output. It is 
worth mentioning that the proper activation/deactivation of a 
TTC requires the middle transistors M2 and M4 to be made N 
times wider than M1, M3, MF1, and MF2, such that maximum 
current flows through them. To illustrate this modification, 
consider the case when X1 and X3 are at high logic level and X2 
is at low logic level. In this condition, TTC2 is activated as M4 
is OFF. Alternatively, in TTC1, both M1 and middle transistor 
M2 are ON. Thus, to allow maximum current to flow through 
the middle transistor M2, it is made N times wider in compar­
ison to the outer transistors M1 and MF1 in TTC.
A PFSCL FC D-­latch is obtained by connecting CLK and 
its complement (CLK) to the middle transistor of TTC1 and 
TTC2, respectively, and connecting input D to TTC1 as shown 
in Figure  1b. The output nodes Q2 and Q4 from TTC1 and 
TTC2, respectively, are combined to form final output Q for 
the ­D-­latch. For a low value of CLK signal, M2 is OFF, and 
M4 is ON, such that TTC1 is activated and TTC2 is deacti­
vated. Because TTC1 is in active state, therefore, any changes 
in input D gets reflected at output node Q. Consequently, for 
a high value of CLK signal, M2 is ON, and M4 is OFF. This

2.2   |   PFSCL Tristate Buffer–Based D-­Latch
A PFSCL tristate buffer can be used to implement a negative 
level–sensitive D-­latch [19, 20] as shown in Figure 2a. It con­
sists of two tristate buffers PB1 and PB2 controlled by com­
plement (CLK) and CLK, respectively. For a low value of CLK 
signal, tristate buffer PB1 is enabled, such that the changes 
in input D are reflected at Q whereas tristate buffer PB2 is 
in high-­impedance state and does not influence the out­
put. Contrary to this, a high value of CLK signal makes PB1 
in high-­impedance state and enables PB2. The last value of 
Q is therefore retained for a high value of CLK signal. The 
­corresponding MOS schematic of a negative level–sensitive 
­D-­latch is shown in Figure 2b. In this D-­latch, for a low value 
of CLK signal, the transistor M6 in PB1 conducts, such that 
the changes in data D are available at node Q. The tristate buf­
fer PB2 has no effect on Q during this period as transistors 
M6s are OFF and the buffer PB2 operates in high-­impedance 
state. Conversely, for a high value of CLK signal, transistor 
M6 does not conduct, and PB1 enters into the high-­impedance 
state while PB2 gets enabled and provides the last value of Q 
as the output.
3   |   Proposed PFSCL Edge-­Triggered Registers
This section presents the design of positive edge-­triggered 
PFSCL registers. Two design approaches, namely, static and 
dynamic register designs, are put forward. Both approaches 
are based on a master–slave configuration as illustrated in 
Figure 3. The master stage receives input data D and tempo­
rarily holds it until the rising edge of a clock signal (CLK). 
At the transition, the master stage transfers the data to the 
slave stage, which retains the data until the next clock edge. 
The static positive edge-­triggered PFSCL register design is il­
lustrated first, followed by a dynamic positive edge-­triggered 
PFSCL register design.
3.1   |   Proposed Static PFSCL Registers
A static register employs feedback to retain its output value 
indefinitely while a dynamic register generally maintains the 
value as charge on a capacitor [24, 25]. Two designs of static 
register are presented by using PFSCL FC (SR-­1) and PFSCL 
tristate buffer (SR-­2)–based D-­latch designs. The positive edge-­
triggered static PFSCL register (SR-­1) is shown in Figure 4a. The

It is worth mentioning that the aforementioned two static 
PFSCL registers have multiple current sources. These sources 
continuously draw bias current, which results in static power 
consumption, computed as the product of the power supply 
and total bias current. Also, both the proposed PFSCL static 
registers have feedback connections to retain the output value. 
The two designs can be improved in terms of power consump­
tion and propagation delay performance by restricting the 
­current flow and facilitating temporary storage of charge to 
lower the gate count. Thus, a new efficient register design 
named as dynamic PFSCL register is presented in the next 
subsection.
3.2   |   Proposed Dynamic PFSCL Registers
The new dynamic PFSCL registers further improve SR-­2 regis­
ters by restricting the bias current flow in order to reduce the 
overall power consumption. The design works on temporary 
storage of charge and eliminates the feedback connection be­
tween the master and slave stages. Thus, the dynamic register 
employs two modified PFSCL tristate buffers in contrast to four 
PFSCL tristate buffers in the SR-­2 design. Three designs of dy­
namic PFSCL registers by modifying the current source section 
are proposed and described further.
The complete MOS schematic of the first PFSCL dynamic regis­
ter (DR-­1) is shown in Figure 5a. It consists of two tristate buf­
fers PB1 and PB2 where the PB1 forms the master stage and PB2 
serves as the slave stage. The current source section of both the 
buffers is modified by inserting a PMOS transistor below the 
current source. The PMOS transistors M7 (in PB1) and M14 (in 
PB2) are driven by CLK and CLK signal, respectively, to control 
the flow of current for reducing the power consumption of each 
buffer. When CLK is low, PB1 samples input D at node X due 
to flow of bias current while PB2 maintains a high-­impedance 
state as no bias current flows. During a low-­to-­high CLK tran­
sition, PB1 enters high-­impedance state and holds the last value 
at node X. The tristate buffer PB2 copies this value to the output 
node Q as bias current starts to flow due to transition. It is worth 
mentioning that the proposed DR-­1 design necessitates a higher 
bias voltage (BIAS) compared to a conventional PFSCL tristate 
buffer to maintain the same current value ISS due to the stacking 
of PMOS transistor below the current source.
The requirement of high voltage for the bias current is further 
eliminated in the second PFSCL dynamic register DR-­2 design 
by placing PMOS transistors above the corresponding current 
sources in PB1 and PB2. The same is depicted in Figure 5b. The 
design DR-­2 achieves similar functionality as DR-­1 but is advan­
tageous as it avoids voltage headroom as observed in the pro­
posed DR-­1 register.
The proposed design-­3 (DR-­3) presents a different mecha­
nism to restrict the flow of current. The availability of bias 
voltage (VBIAS) to the current source is made dependent on 
either CLK or CLK signal by using a PMOS M8 transistor and a 
NMOS M7 transistor of tristate buffer PB1 shown in Figure 5c. 
When CLK is low, PB1 is activated as transistors M5, M6, and 
M8 are switched ON. Consequently, input D is sampled to 
node X. At the same time, PB2 is in high-­impedance state 
because the transistors M13, M14, and M16 are switched OFF. 
During a low-­to-­high transition on CLK signal, PB1 en­
ters high-­impedance state, ceasing the sampling of input D 
and transitioning into the hold mode. Simultaneously, buf­
fer PB2 is enabled, copying the content of X to output Q. In 
this design, PB1 and PB2 buffers do not consume power in a 
high-­impedance state as the potential of nodes Y and Y1 is dis­
charged to ground potential, which consequently disable their 
current sources.
4   |   Simulation and Discussion
In this section, the functionality of the proposed static and dy­
namic PFSCL register designs is verified through simulations 
in LTspice using PTM 90-­nm CMOS technology parameters. 
The power supply, current source, voltage swing, and load ca­
pacitance of 1.1 V, 400 mV, 100 μA, and 50 fF, respectively, are 
taken. Thereafter, the performance of the different proposed 
1-­bit registers is compared with the existing static CMOS posi­
tive edge-­triggered register (ER), and dynamic CMOS registers 
that include C2MOS register, dual-­edge register, and true single-­
phase clocked register (TSPC) are considered. The schematic of

4.3   |   Clock Overlap Issue in Static PFSCL Register
A register design is usually based on employing perfect CLK and 
CLK signals. However, in practical scenarios, achieving perfect 
clock inversion signals is challenging because of different rout­
ing paths [22, 26]. This condition results in overlapping CLK pe­
riods, termed as 0–0 and 1–1 overlaps, which leads to undesired 
behavior. In this subsection, the issue of clock overlap in the pro­
posed registers is discussed, and thereafter, methods to address 
the clock overlap issue are suggested.

The proposed PFSCL dynamic register, DR-­2, is considered to il­
lustrate the clock overlap issue. A closer examination of the DR-­2 
reveals that the setup time (tsetup) is simply the propagation delay 
of PB1 td_PB1 and corresponds to the time taken to sample the 
input D to node X. The hold time (thold) is approximately zero be­
cause PB1 is turned OFF on the CLK edge, and further changes 
in the input are ignored.
During the 0–0 overlap period, the CLK-­ and CLK-­driven tran­
sistors M6, M13, M7, and M14, as indicated by the red tick mark 
in Figure 12a, conduct, such that any changes in input D are 
reflected at the register output node Q. After 0–0 overlap pe­
riod, CLK becomes 1. If data sampled during 0–0 overlap have 
reached X, then wrong data will be reflected at the output. Thus, 
0–0 overlap is conflict, and data should be stable during overlap 
period. In such situation, any changes in D reach the output of 
register, provided that the delay from D to Q is more than 0–0 
overlap. Thus, the circuit malfunctions as it fails to maintain the 
last value at its output Q. Conversely, for a 1–1 overlap period, 
the CLK-­ and CLK-­driven transistors M6, M13, M7, and M14, as 
indicated in Figure 12b by a blue tick mark, are turned OFF, 
such that any changes in input D are not reflected at the register 
output node Q, and the last value is maintained. After 1–1 over­
lap, CLK becomes 0, and the master stage becomes transparent, 
resulting X to follow input D. The respective timing waveform of 
the proposed PFSCL DR-­2 register as shown in Figure 12c vali­
dates the theoretical prepositions. Thus, it is clear that there is a 
need to address these overlap issues.

4.4   |   Design Example
A 3-­bit shift register is considered as a design example to demon­
strate the effectiveness of the proposals. The block diagram of 
a 3-­bit shift register is shown in Figure 15a. A different 3-­bit 
shift register is implemented by employing the proposed PFSCL 
and existing CMOS registers. The design of a 3-­bit shift register 
using the proposed PFSCL DR-­2 register is shown in Figure 15b 
for illustration. It is constructed by connecting three PFSCL 
DR-­2 registers (R1, R2, and R3) in series, where the output of 
the first register (R1) becomes the input to the second register 
(R2) and so on. For a low value of the CLK signal, PB1 is en­
abled while PB2 is in a high-­impedance state in the R1 register. 
In this condition, the changes in input are available at node X1 
but are not transferred to output node Q1 as PB2 is in a high-­
impedance state. Conversely, for a high value of the CLK signal, 
PB1 exhibits a hold state while PB2 provides the last value of Q1 
as the output of R1. The data stored in each register are trans­
ferred to the next register in the chain as the next CLK arrives. 
As a result, the data propagates in a serial fashion, with each 
bit moving one position to the right. The timing diagram of the 
proposed 3-­bit shift register using the PFSCL DR-­2 register is 
shown in Figure 15c.

5   |   Conclusion
This paper presents design approaches for the design of PFSCL 
edge-­triggered registers suited for high-­performance computing 
systems. The first approach is static in nature and maintains a flow 
of constant current throughout the operation. Two static register 
designs employing PFSCL fundamental cell (SR-­1) and PFSCL tri­
state buffer (SR-­2) are proposed. The second approach is dynamic 
and improves the performance of PFSCL register by restricting 
the current flow and facilitating temporary storage of charge. 
Three designs for dynamic PFSCL registers (DR-­1)–(DR-­3) are 
put forward. The performance of the proposed PFSCL registers 
is compared with existing CMOS registers through simulations in 
LTspice using PTM 90-­nm CMOS technology parameters, with 
layouts drawn in the Microwind tool. The performance compar­
ison reveals the superior performance of the proposed PFSCL 
registers in terms of performance parameters such as propaga­
tion delay, power consumption, PDP, and area. The proposed 
PFSCL DR-­2 register shows significant improvements of 52.7%, 
93.8%, and 97% in propagation delay, power consumption, and 
PDP values in comparison to the existing CMOS registers with 
59% area overhead, respectively. Additionally, Monte Carlo and 
corner analysis indicates that the proposed DR-­2 register exhibits 
the least variation in propagation delay of 2.98%, confirming their 
stability across process fluctuations. This paper also addresses 
the clock overlap issue in the proposed register to achieve clock 
skew insensitivity. Lastly, a 3-­bit shift register implementation is 
included as a design example.

Abstract: This paper presents the design of edge-­triggered PFSCL registers for high-­performance computing systems employed in mixed-­signal applications. Two different approaches named as static and dynamic for register design are presented. The static approach maintains a constant current flow in the register design throughout the operation. Two static register designs em­ ploying either PFSCL fundamental cells (FC) (SR1) or PFSCL tristate buffers (SR2) are proposed. The proposed static registers have high power consumption and gate count. Alternatively, a dynamic register design approach that restricts the current flow and facilitates the temporary storage of charge is proposed. Three designs for dynamic PFSCL registers (DR-­1, DR-­2, and DR-­3) are proposed. All the proposed PFSCL and existing CMOS registers are implemented and simulated in LTspice with layouts drawn in the Microwind tool. The performance comparison indicates that the PFSCL registers show improved performance over existing CMOS counterparts at high operating frequency. Further, it is found that the proposed PFSCL DR-­2 register achieves the best performance by attaining the maximum improvements of 52.7%, 93.8%, and 97% in propagation delay, power, and PDP values at 1 GHz, respectively, as compared to the existing CMOS registers with 59% area overhead. The Monte Carlo and corner analysis confirm the stability of the proposed PFSCL registers against process variations and identify the proposed DR-­2 register as the least prone design to variations. This paper also addresses the clock overlap issue in the proposed register and presents different methods to achieve clock skew insensitivity. Lastly, a 3-­bit shift register implementation is included as a design example.
